Mayr's equation

Herbert Mayr's group at LMU Munich measured the rates of thousands of reactions between nucleophiles and electrophiles and found that one short equation describes them, at 20 °C:

log k = sN (N + E)log k₂₀ °C, with k the second-order rate constant in M⁻¹ s⁻¹

N
the nucleophilicity of the nucleophile. It belongs to the nucleophile in one solvent: the same anion has different N values in water and in DMSO.
sN
the sensitivity of that nucleophile, the slope of its line below. Most values lie between about 0.5 and 1.2.
E
the electrophilicity of the electrophile, treated as independent of the solvent.

Because log k = 0 when E = −N, a nucleophile's N is minus the E of an electrophile it attacks with k = 1 M⁻¹ s⁻¹. The parameters of a few hundred electrophiles and more than a thousand nucleophiles are collected in Mayr's Database of Reactivity Parameters, where every card in this app links to its entry.

How N, sN and E are measured

Mayr and Patz fixed the scales in 1994 with two definitions: E = 0 for the bis(4-methoxyphenyl)methylium ion, and sN = 1 for 2-methylpent-1-ene. Benzhydrylium ions Ar₂CH⁺ and quinone methides, whose reactivity can be tuned over a wide range by changing their substituents, became the reference electrophiles.

  1. A new nucleophile is combined with several reference electrophiles of known E, and each rate constant k is measured, usually by following the coloured electrophile by UV–vis spectroscopy.
  2. Plotting log k against E gives a straight line. Its slope is sN, and the E where it crosses log k = 0 is −N.
  3. A new electrophile is measured the other way round, against reference nucleophiles of known N and sN: each gives E = log k / sN − N, and the values are averaged.

In 2012 the whole benzhydrylium data set was refitted (Ammer, Nolte and Mayr); the database, and this app, use the current values.

Reading the numbers

  • The −5 rule of thumb. When sN is ignored, a pair reacts at room temperature if N + E > −5. That is the rule behind Reacting?; the feedback then works out log k with sN.
  • The fast end. Near k = 10⁹–10¹⁰ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ reactions become diffusion-controlled: every encounter reacts, the equation stops working (above about 10⁸) and selectivity is lost.
  • One solvent at a time. N depends strongly on the solvent, especially for anions, which water and alcohols solvate by hydrogen bonding. The nitromethane anion has N = 20.71 in DMSO but 12.06 in water. Rank therefore only compares nucleophiles measured in the same solvent; E values can be compared across all sets.
  • Crossing lines. Two nucleophiles with different sN can swap order depending on the electrophile, as two lines in the chart above can cross. Ranking by N alone, as in Rank, is Mayr's own first approximation.
  • Where the equation works. It was built for reactions in which one new bond forms and steric effects are small. Bulky partners (a trityl cation with a hindered amine) and SN2 reactions at alkyl halides are less well described.

Which atom reacts

Many nucleophiles have more than one nucleophilic atom (enolates, cyanide, thiocyanate, pyridones, amino alcohols), and many electrophiles more than one electrophilic atom (enones, molecules with two carbonyl groups). For ambident reactivity Mayr, Breugst and Ofial (2011) replaced the hard and soft acids and bases (HSAB) rule with three questions:

  1. Is the reaction reversible? Then the more stable product wins (thermodynamic control): N-attack of thiocyanate, C-alkylation of enamines.
  2. If not, which site is faster? Marcus theory splits the barrier into an intrinsic part and the reaction's driving force. Reactions with high intrinsic barriers, such as SN2 at carbon, follow the more stable product even under kinetic control: enolates are C-alkylated by alkyl halides.
  3. Is it diffusion-controlled? Then every encounter reacts and there is no selectivity: very reactive carbocations attack cyanide at both ends.

For regioselectivity in addition, substitution and elimination reactions, the same two ideas, the stability of the cation, anion or radical formed and kinetic against thermodynamic control, explain most of the questions in the Regioselectivity tab. Each answer comes with a short reason.

Computed indices: ω and N from orbital energies

Mayr's parameters are measured. Computational chemists often estimate reactivity instead from a single calculation per molecule, with the conceptual DFT indices. With Koopmans' approximation, the ionisation energy is I ≈ −εHOMO and the electron affinity A ≈ −εLUMO, and:

μ = (εHOMO + εLUMO) / 2
electronic chemical potential: how strongly the molecule holds on to its electrons (Parr and Pearson 1983).
η = εLUMO − εHOMO
chemical hardness: resistance to charge transfer. Some authors include a factor ½; Domingo's scales below leave it out.
ω = μ² / (2η)
global electrophilicity index: the energy gained when the molecule takes up as much electron density from its surroundings as it can (Parr, von Szentpály and Liu 1999).
N = εHOMO(Nu) − εHOMO(TCE)
Domingo's nucleophilicity index, measured from the HOMO of tetracyanoethylene computed at the same level of theory (B3LYP/6-31G(d) in the published scales), so that it is positive for nearly all nucleophiles (Domingo, Chamorro and Pérez 2008).
Class (Domingo 2016)Electrophiles, ωNucleophiles, N
Strong> 1.5 eV> 3.0 eV
Moderate0.8–1.5 eV2.0–3.0 eV
Marginal< 0.8 eV< 2.0 eV

The inverse of the electrophilicity, 1/ω, is sometimes used as a nucleophilicity index. It follows nucleophilicity only within limited series of molecules (it fails, for example, for captodative ethylenes), so the thresholds above are for Domingo's N.

Local versions: which atom

Condensed Fukui functions split a global index over the atoms. From the atomic charges qk of the molecule with N, N+1 and N−1 electrons, all at the neutral geometry: fk⁺ = qk(N) − qk(N+1) marks the atoms that nucleophiles attack, and fk⁻ = qk(N−1) − qk(N) the atoms that attack electrophiles (Yang and Mortier 1986). Domingo's Parr functions use the atomic spin densities of the radical anion (Pk⁺) and radical cation (Pk⁻) instead, giving local indices ωk = ω·Pk⁺ and Nk = N·Pk⁻.

How the two kinds of number relate

The conceptual DFT indices describe one isolated molecule from one calculation; Mayr's parameters are rate constants measured in solution, with solvation and steric effects included. They tend to agree within a family of similar molecules, but they are not on the same scale: Mayr's N and Domingo's N share a letter and nothing else.
